newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan "sokaiya" threat signals need for reform.
newsitem.headline: Japan "sokaiya" threat signals need for reform.

text.p: In Japanese corporate tradition, shareholders should be seen but not heard.

But while police are mobilising to help firms fend off "sokaiya" extortionists at shareholders' meetings on Friday, critics say what's needed is reform of the secretive practices that leave management prey to threats and breed scandals.

Japanese firms have long bunched their annual shareholders' meetings on the same day to avoid being hassled by sokaiya, corporate extortionists who target such events, and in some cases to muzzle questions from legitimate shareholders as well.
This year is no exception.

Some 2,300 firms are set to hold shareholders' gatherings on Friday, among them the giant brokerage Nomura Securities and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank, which have both been rocked by allegations of close ties and huge payoffs to a sokaiya.
The recent rash of scandals, however, has fuelled calls to reform management methods which fail to hold executives accountable and give short shrift to shareholders' interests.

Sokaiya, who are often but not always linked to crime syndicates, try to extort money from firms by threatening to expose dubious business practices or stir up trouble at shareholders' meetings, which firms anyway regard as more of a ceremony than a forum for briefing investors.

Police say sokaiya numbers have dwindled to around 1,000 from about 1,700 in 1983, when a ban on payoffs took effect, and have loudly urged companies to take the plunge and stop further dealings with the racketeers.

"We want companies to be deeply aware of the trend at home and abroad which is demanding corporate fairness and transparency," said National Police Agency official Toshio Tamatsukuri in a newspaper interview this week. "Now is the time to boldly cut ties with sokaiya."
Critics, however, argue firms would not be vulnerable to racketeer threats if they were not guilty of misdeeds and, more critically, inclined more toward disclosure than cover-ups.

The opacity of Japanese corporate decision-making and the disregard for shareholders' interests are increasingly under fire as Tokyo undertakes a mammoth deregulation programme for its financial sector and other industries.

"The responsibility of Japanese management has been shrouded in anonymity," said a recent article in the Nihon Keizai Shimbun financial daily. "A distorted management concept has spread that sees it as necessary to hide important information that touches on the foundation of management."

"But as the market's capability to act in a supervisory role grows (along with deregulation), the risk for companies of hiding information will grow bigger than the risk of disclosure," the newspaper said.
For now, however, while some Japanese shareholders are fed up with management misdeeds and even willing to seek recourse in the courts, the outspoken remain the minority.

"Individual Japanese shareholders have no concept of participating in management. All most of them care about is whether the share price goes up," said Tokuo Sakaguchi, a member of Shareholders Ombudsman, a group of lawyers, accountants and shareholders monitoring corporate activities.

"And institutional investors don't attack management behaviour in public at shareholders' meetings because of the cross-shareholding structure," the lawyer said. "What we need is pressure from overseas investors."
Such pressure, as well as from domestic institutional investors, is likely to mount, but it is unclear how quickly.

A U.S. investor service, Institutional Shareholder Services, has urged Nomura shareholders to reject the scandal-plagued company's team of internal auditors to be voted on at its Friday shareholders' meeting.
Japan analyst Bruce Babcock urged shareholders in a June 16 report by the investor service to press Nomura to appoint truly independent auditors who could forestall any future scandals.

CalPERS (California's Public Employees' Retirement System), America's biggest public pension fund, will likely "step up action" here after unveiling corporate governance principles for the country later this year, a CalPERS spokesman said.

But spokesman Brad Pacheco added: "I don't think we're in a position right now to do what we've done in the U.K. or France, or for that matter the United States," where CalPERS governance principles are already in place.
